historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Carbamate skeletal muscle relaxants

starting.description: Existing glycerol ethers had observed skeletal-muscle-relaxant effects: Berger and Bradley documented the related mephenesin effect, while the glyceryl guaiacolate parent of methocarbamol was also described as muscle-relaxing. Murphey explicitly used these known active compounds as the prior-art context for a new carbamate.

inspiration.description: Previously observed muscle-relaxing activity of related glycerol ethers, including mephenesin and glyceryl guaiacolate; the latter was the chemical parent of methocarbamol. An existing mephenesin carbamate was also prior art. No claim is made that a natural material motivated the program.

steps.description: Following observed muscle relaxation in a glycerol-ether series, Berger and Bradley selected myanesin for pharmacological and preliminary clinical evaluation.

By 1951 Ginzel had compared the related myanesin with Myokain, o-methoxyphenyl glycerol ether, for central paralytic and anticonvulsant effects, among other properties. A later contemporary account identifies the glyceryl guaiacolate parent of methocarbamol as muscle relaxing.

Murphey described prior active glycerol-ether relaxants and proposed an ortho-alkoxy-substituted carbamate series, including the glyceryl-guaiacolate carbamate, to seek improved duration and reduced adverse hemolytic action.
A 1958 pharmacological comparison identified AHR-85 as methocarbamol and reported longer protection for the carbamate than its glycerol-ether parent in a rat strychnine-challenge assay.

design.description: Murphey carbamylated the terminal hydroxyl of an active glycerol-ether parent, using an ortho-alkoxy-substituted aromatic structure, with the stated goals of prolonging activity and reducing adverse hemolytic action. This is deliberate structural optimization of active leads, not evidence of a de novo therapeutic concept.

circumstances.description: The specific event described as planned is Murphey's carbamate-development objective; whether the initial observation of relaxation was unexpected is not established by the cited original study.

limits: The established causal chain is bounded to methocarbamol, the sole cohort member: its chemical parent is glyceryl guaiacolate. Mephenesin was a related working relaxant, not the chemical parent used in Murphey’s example.

Mephenesin carbamate was already prior art in the patent; its own discovery sequence and other carbamate relaxant branches are not reconstructed here. Do not extrapolate the methocarbamol pathway to all later carbamate compounds.
conflicts: S3 cites Ginzel and colleagues’ Ueber Tierversuche mit Myocain as 1948;99:229, whereas S6 PubMed metadata and S5’s bibliography give 1949;99:299. The original was not read; no priority claim depends on resolving this citation error.
For S5, PubMed metadata lists pages 330–338, while the publisher lists 331–338; the publisher pagination is used in the citation.
gaps: The 1949 Ginzel and colleagues Myocain report was located as metadata only and not read; the complete 1951 Ginzel paper and 1958 Truitt–Little report were accessible only as publisher summaries or abstracts.

The earliest discovery circumstances and priority of glyceryl guaiacolate’s relaxant effect, and whether that initial finding was unexpected, are not established. S3 attributes parent activity to Ginzel; S5 supplies the 1951 original summary.
The patent’s stated objectives and reported pharmacological comparisons are not independent evidence of comparative clinical efficacy, duration or safety.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: Prior muscle-relaxant use, short duration and blood-damage or hematuria concerns motivated a search for longer-acting carbamates with fewer unwanted effects.
humanContributionInterpretation.scope: The patent mixes animal work, blood assays and human measurements; this is a broad clinical-precedent link rather than an exclusively bedside origin.
